# openhamclock

**Community continuation of HamClock as a browser dashboard — grey line, propagation, spots, satellites**

- **Version recorded:** 26.7.0
- **Categories:** `hf-propagation`
- **Upstream:** <https://github.com/accius/openhamclock>

## What it does

Serves a live station dashboard in your browser: a world map with the grey line, solar and geomagnetic indices, band-condition predictions, DX cluster and POTA spots, satellite passes, and live decodes from WSJT-X on the same machine. It is the community's continuation of HamClock after its author became a Silent Key in January 2026, rewritten as a web application so it runs on anything with a browser — a shack PC, a Pi driving a wall display, or a phone on the same network if you choose to allow that.

## Why you would want it

It is the at-a-glance answer to "which band should I be on right now", and the more active of the two maintained HamClock successors by a wide margin (Q-006). The alternative is `hamclock-next`, an SDL2 rewrite that keeps the original's look and runs as an ordinary desktop program with no Node involved; both are carried, and `propagation` ships this one as the default.

## Before it will work

**Node.js 20.19 or newer from your distribution** — `hammunition` installs `nodejs` and `npm` from the archive and refuses, naming the version, if what is offered is too old. Debian 13 and Parrot ship 20.19 and Ubuntu 26.04 ships 22.22; **Ubuntu 24.04 ships 18.19 and is refused** — the server needs `require()` of an ES module, which arrived in 20.19, and on 18 it builds and then dies at its first start (measured). The engine will not fetch a newer Node for you (D-037); on 24.04 the answer is `hamclock-next`, or a newer release of the distribution. **A network connection at install time**: the build fetches about 730 packages from registry.npmjs.org, each checked against the lock file that arrives inside the sha256-verified source archive; nothing else is fetched and no package's install scripts run. After installing, **edit `~/.local/share/hammunition/node/openhamclock/.env`** and set `CALLSIGN` and `LOCATOR` — the first start creates that file from upstream's example with `N0CALL` and `FN31` in it, and the dashboard is centred on the wrong hemisphere until you do. A reinstall or update keeps your `.env`. The engine does not fill those values in yet (station config, D-035, is absolute-path config files only so far); this is a hand step and the profile says so.

## How it installs

- node (needs Node 20.19+ from the distribution; dependencies fetched from registry.npmjs.org against the lock file) from https://github.com/accius/openhamclock/archive/refs/tags/v26.7.0.tar.gz
  - build dependencies: `nodejs`, `npm`, `patch`
  - Needs Node.js 20.19 or newer from the distribution's own `nodejs` package — the engine never fetches Node from NodeSource or nodejs.org, and refuses at plan time when the archive's Node is absent or too old. Ubuntu 24.04's 18.19 is too old: it builds, then the server dies at start (ERR_REQUIRE_ESM; measured 2026-09-02), so that target is refused. The build downloads its dependency closure from registry.npmjs.org, verified against the lock file. Built and run 2026-09-02 on Debian 13 (Node 20.19.2, npm 9.2).

## Known problems

**Upstream ignores its own `HOST` setting, so this build patches one line.** v26.7.0 reads `HOST`, prints it, and then listens on `0.0.0.0` anyway — measured, not assumed — which would put a dashboard with an open write API on every interface of a machine that may also carry security tooling. The patch makes `app.listen` use `HOST`, and it is in the manifest for review. With it, the bind is whatever `.env` says: the wrapper sets `HOST=127.0.0.1` but openhamclock's own `.env` loader overrides the environment, and the `.env` it generates says `HOST=localhost`, which Node binds as `::1` — loopback either way, and why the launcher opens `http://localhost:3001` rather than an IPv4 address. Set `HOST=0.0.0.0` in `.env` and the dashboard is reachable from your whole network, which is what you want for a wall display and not what you want on a laptop; the choice is yours and it is one line, and set `API_WRITE_KEY` there if you make it. The same override applies to `PORT`: the launcher opens `:3001`, so change it in `.env` and the browser tab points at the old one. **UDP 2237 listens on every interface regardless** — the WSJT-X integration binds `0.0.0.0` at start and `HOST` does not govern it; set `WSJTX_ENABLED=false` in `.env` if you do not run WSJT-X, or want nothing listening. **The server opens outbound connections the moment it starts** — a persistent telnet session to `telnet.reversebeacon.net:7000` for RBN spots among them, logging in with your `CALLSIGN`, or with the project's own `K0CJH-3` while `.env` still says `N0CALL` (upstream does this deliberately, to keep invalid logins off other people's infrastructure); one more reason to set your callsign before the first start. **Propagation runs in "Standalone mode"**: upstream's build normally downloads an ITU P.533 model as WASM from a moving release tag with a checksum from the same place, which is not a pin, so this build skips it and the server uses its built-in model. A pinned WASM may be carried later as a verified artefact. **The auto-update setting does nothing here**: `AUTO_UPDATE_ENABLED` expects a git clone; leave it `false` and update through `hammunition`, which rebuilds from the next pinned release. The runtime tree is about 180 MB. **Two commands land on your PATH**: `openhamclock` opens the dashboard in a terminal and a browser; `openhamclock-server` is the bare server for a headless box or a systemd unit of your own.

## Keeping it current

- probe: github release (`accius/openhamclock`)
- strategy: rebuild
- Upstream releases monthly, on the first Tuesday (its CHANGELOG says so; the changelog itself is frozen and release notes live on GitHub). A rebuild keeps the operator's .env.
